prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single-achievement prize after reading the full first round and the chair's summary. The structure is the one I think the committee should reward: a sharp prediction in 2011 that a geometric parameter, the twist angle, produces nearly flat bands, and an experiment seven years later that found correlated insulators and superconductivity exactly where the theory pointed. The phenomenology is not in dispute by anyone, including those who rank it below the clock, and it has been reproduced by independent groups in many moire systems, so the real question is not whether the effect exists but whether the committee is willing to recognise a discovery before its explanation is complete. I think it is, and the citation can be worded around the prediction and the observation without any claim about pairing mechanism. The chair's synthesis says the unsettled mechanism is the main objection and that no member doubts reproducibility; I read that as a difference in how much interpretive maturity to demand, not a difference over the facts. The credit is also compact: MacDonald and Bistritzer wrote the prediction and Jarillo-Herrero led the decisive experiment. I have not moved to the lattice clock, although I am now closer to it than in round 1 and would not oppose it, for the reasons given below.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against my choice is the one my colleagues have pressed: after about eight years the pairing mechanism, the phase diagram and the sensitivity to twist-angle disorder are still debated, and the experimental credit cannot be made complete with one experimental name, since Cao, Fatemi and the Dean, Young and Kim groups did important parallel and follow-up work. Seven of eight members prefer the lattice clock, which has quantitatively confirmed performance across independent laboratories, a clean two-name credit and no maturity concern. I should not dismiss that convergence as mere counting, because several of those colleagues moved after weighing the same attribution and maturity arguments I weigh, and the atomic-physics members can assess the clock's systematics in a way I cannot. If the committee judges that a prize should wait until the interpretation settles, my preferred configuration is the weaker one this year, and a later cycle would lose little.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from twisted bilayer graphene to the lattice clock, saying the unsettled mechanism and eight-year age of the field moved him most, while still calling the phenomenology secure and not premature in the sense that the effect might disappear.
responses.response: I agree with you that the phenomenology is secure and that the citation should say nothing about mechanism, and I am glad you do not call the case premature. Where I differ is that I do not think an open mechanism should weigh so heavily in the choice between the two. A prize for the discovery of flat-band-driven correlated phases does not depend on the answer to the pairing question, and the chair notes that nobody raises reproducibility as a doubt. I also take your point that choosing the clock is a judgment in favour of maturity over opening, and I do not think you made that choice carelessly. I hold my position, but I accept that our difference is one of timing and not of scientific merit.

responses.point: Lindroth rates the clock first and twisted bilayer graphene a strong alternative, but proposed only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, treating Bistritzer's inclusion as a junior-credit question, and asks the committee to wait for the pairing mechanism to settle.
responses.response: The chair asked whether Bistritzer belongs, and my answer is yes. The 2011 prediction is a two-author paper whose first author is Bistritzer, and a prize for the prediction that omits him would credit the idea to one of the two people who published it. A three-person limit leaves room, so the cost of including him is that I must accept the experimental side is thin, which I do. On waiting for the mechanism, I would answer that the committee has recognised discoveries whose explanation arrived afterwards, and an uncertain mechanism is a reason for careful wording rather than delay. I do agree with you that the clock case rests on atomic-structure understanding I cannot check myself.

responses.point: Eriksson moved to the lattice clock in round 1 after weighing attribution and maturity, and argued that the clock's two decades of independent confirmation outweigh twisted bilayer graphene's eight years and the larger experimental team behind it.
responses.response: Your argument about confirmation across laboratories is the strongest one against me, and I do not claim that twisted bilayer graphene matches the clock on quantitative agreement. My disagreement is that the length of the record is a measure of a different thing. The graphene result has been reproduced qualitatively by many independent groups within a few years, which is what establishes a discovery, whereas the clock's record establishes performance. Your own case against the clock, that it is primarily metrological and builds on 2005 and 2012, is the reason I keep returning to the discovery question and it is not answered by saying the attribution is cleaner.

responses.point: Kroll argues that discovery versus instrument should not be a hard line, citing Charpak and Hall-Haensch as precedents for measurement inventions, and that the nuclear clock is too immature to split Ye's credit.
responses.response: I accept both points. The precedents show the committee does recognise measurement inventions that change what can be tested, and I withdraw any suggestion that the thorium work should reduce Ye's credit now. What I still ask is the chair's first question, which is what distinguishes the lattice clock from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and I would want the answer to be that the new physics has already been delivered, not that it is expected. If the committee can write that scope statement with specific results (constraints on constants, millimetre-scale redshift measurements), I would regard the clock as a defensible prize, and I say so plainly rather than hold out for consensus either way.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, pushed back on my first-place Event Horizon Telescope choice in round 1, saying attribution within a roughly 300-person collaboration and model-dependent gravity tests make it a weaker prize candidate.
responses.response: You were right and I said so in round 1, and I have not changed that view. I keep the Event Horizon Telescope as an alternative because the shadow image is a discovery in the plain sense, but I would not lead with a three-name split that depends on contested conventions about who led a very large collaboration. On attribution, I think twisted bilayer graphene is cleaner than the Event Horizon Telescope, because the theory credit is two named authors on a single paper and the experimental credit is one group leader, with the acknowledged gap in the early-career authors.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is prepared to recognise the phenomenon before the pairing mechanism is understood, or regards that as the deciding maturity question this cycle.
How much the exclusion of Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire groups should weigh against a three-name credit that is otherwise clean.

Whether the committee can write a scope statement for the lattice clock that separates it from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on the basis of results already delivered, which would change my assessment of B025.
I rely on my recollection of the chronology and of the clock uncertainty figures and have not checked them against primary papers.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B022, B025 or B054. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of the credited names appears among them. I am a theorist in high-energy physics and gravitation, not in condensed matter or atomic physics, so I defer to colleagues with direct expertise on the clock systematics and on the electronic structure of moire systems. As Secretary I note that I have no stake in the outcome beyond the procedure.
